# Itiha intelligence brief, 2026-11-26

**The Indonesia long-form drew more views on its seventh day than on its fourth and is close to becoming the channel's fifth breakout, so its Bali follow-up stays first. Today is the last day for the Guru Tegh Bahadur Short: write it tonight or press Drop, and give tomorrow to Churchill, due in four days with nothing written.**

## This week: 3 decisions
1. **Script and publish a follow-up long-form for the Indonesia video's viewers: why Bali stayed Hindu when Java converted.** (long, due 2026-12-02, open since 2026-11-19)  
   Why: The Indonesia long-form is still growing: 118,064 views in 8 days, more on day seven than day four, and 3.9 subscribers per 1,000 views against 2 for the Asia one. The follow-up should reach those viewers while they still come. Bali as the subject is a guess from the comments.  
   First step: Still nothing on disk. Add the Indonesia transcript to the library today and read the line at 0:19, where most viewers leave. Then pick the culprit and the date for sentence one. Keep “Indonesia” in the title.
2. **Script and publish a Short for Churchill's birthday on 30 November: what his War Cabinet was told about the Bengal famine in 1943, and what it decided.** (short, due 2026-11-30, open since 2026-11-24)  
   Why: Four days out, nothing on disk. You made one on this before: “Churchill Refused Netaji's offer | Bengal Famine 1943” lost viewers at 0:05 when it stopped to explain the INA. Its lesson: “The one-sentence context rule applies inside the first 10 seconds most of all.” A ruler convicted by his own papers is the channel's best shape for subscribers. That the birthday lifts it is a guess.  
   First step: Today: read the 1943 War Cabinet minutes and Amery's diary, pick one document and its date, and open on it. Record by 28 November and publish the morning of 30 November, his name first in the title.
3. **Script and publish a Short on Aurangzeb's order to execute Guru Tegh Bahadur, for 24 November.** (short, due 2026-11-24, open since 2026-11-15)  
   Why: Two days past its date, nothing on disk, and it lapses on its own tomorrow. Late, it keeps only its search value: people look up “guru tegh bahadur history” all year. That is worth less than today's hours on the Churchill Short, which is due in four days and not written.  
   First step: Decide today. Either write and publish it tonight, his name first in the title and Aurangzeb's order in sentence one, or press Drop with a one-line note. Do not let it eat into the Churchill recording.

Everything below is the evidence. Mark a decision done or dropped on the Brief tab; an open one stays here until then.

## Channel health
18,400 subscribers, up 600 in a week, against 100,000 by 28 September 2027. November's milestone is 20,840, which needs 84.5 net a day. The last 7 days ran at 99, above that pace, and the last 28 at 63.2; the channel is still 2,076 behind the ramp, so on the 7-day rate November ends near 18,796, 2,044 short. Videos brought 51.2% of net subscribers over 28 days, just over half; the rest came with no video attached. Furthest behind is breakouts: none this month against 1,956 subscribers planned from them, and one video of the usual breakout size (1,396) closes most of the gap. Growth here comes in jumps: breakouts carry 63.8% of lifetime subscribers. The nearest one is the Indonesia long-form, at 409 against the breakout line of 500, still adding about 40 a day. Last week the long-form you picked yourself beat its usual, which is why its follow-up leads this week.

What's working
- “How the Ramayana Was REWRITTEN to Convert Hindus” is holding: it drew more views on its seventh day than on its fourth and pushed long-form views up 161.8% week over week. Over 28 days long-form earns 86.4% of the net subscribers videos bring; over the 365-day window, 82.9%, at 7.49x as many subscribers per view as Shorts.
- The best subscriber-earner of the 90-day window is still “How One Man Who Never Visited India Wrote Its History”, 12.4 net per 1,000 views: a villain convicted by his own paycheck. The Churchill Short is built the same way.
- The two Shorts since the film run are liked well above the usual Short: “How British Officers Lived Like Kings on Indian Land Tax” at 8.0% and “Why Portuguese Goa Taxed Every Hindu's SHIKHA” at 6.2%, against 3.9% for the median Short. Colonial tax stories land with the viewers who see them.

What's wrong
- Viewers leave the Indonesia long-form early: average view is 27.7%, and the biggest drop comes at 0:19, where 16 points of the audience go. What is said there cannot be read, because its transcript is still not in the library. Only 41.6% of November's long-form views were engaged views, and over the 365-day window long-form now brings 7.2 subscribers per 1,000 views, below its usual range. Probable cause: Home-feed plays that are not real viewing, and an opening that has not reached its culprit by 0:19. Test: read the line at 0:19 once the transcript is in; the Bali script names its culprit before then.
- Shorts views fell 84.3% week over week (21,353 against 136,189). That is the film run ending, not new Shorts failing: the two posted since 22 November are at the channel's usual. It also changed where Shorts are found: search now brings only 32.2% of Shorts views over 28 days, under half. Test, still open: the Malay Ravana Short is not up yet; if its first day runs slower than the Goa shikha Short's 33.4 views an hour, no more film Shorts.
- A viewer's fact-check under the Indonesia video says several supporting facts are wrong and questions the main argument, that sultans deliberately rewrote the Ramayana. Probable cause: the script leaned on one Malay text for a claim about intent. Test: answer it with sources this week; if a point is wrong, pin the correction before the Bali video goes up, because it goes to the same viewers.
- “Why Sonia Gandhi NEVER Forgave Narasimha Rao” has 1,000 views and no subscribers, below the usual for its kind, even though viewers stayed (80.6% average view). Probable cause: party politics, the kind of Short that does worst here. No test needed; it is why the Tipu row below is a skip.

## Audience
Analytics runs to 2026-11-23. Long-form is found on Home: 255,116 of its 285,187 views over 28 days came through Home and the subscriptions feed, against 7,307 from search, so a long-form's title and thumbnail have to win on Home. Outside YouTube, WhatsApp sends the most viewers: 12,970 views over the 365-day window, 27.8x what Instagram sends.
- A Malaysian viewer adds what the Indonesia video left out: “The other part is that the European colonisation actually helped expedite the locals' conversion to Islam.” The Bali script should check what the Dutch and Portuguese did on Java and Bali before it names a culprit.
- Caribbean Hindus are watching. Under the same video: “This is still happening in my birth country Guyana to poor people.” That is the first idea below.
- Viewers read the colonial Shorts as being about today. Under the British officers' Short: “Same with today's Bureaucracy too.”

## How they are reacting
The Indonesia long-form still holds the week's comments: viewers from Indonesia and Malaysia adding and correcting, a long fact-check, anger at Islam as a whole, and a smaller pushback that every religion does this.
- **Viewers in Malaysia and Indonesia filling in the story** (mixed): "A Malaysian here. This is true, but only part of the whole story."
- **A point-by-point fact-check of the Indonesia video** (negative): "Fact checking - there are many mistakes"
- **Anger turning on Islam as a whole** (negative): "Everytime I learn more about Islam, it sounds like Sauron levels of evil maipulation"
- **Every religion rewrites stories** (mixed): "All religions do this, like brahmins rewrite a jataka/folk tale"
- **Diaspora Hindus seeing it in their own countries** (mixed): "This is still happening in my birth country Guyana to poor people."

Requested topics
- Rajendra Chola's raid on Srivijaya
- A Krishna video in the shape of the Asia Ramayana one
- Bagan and Hindu influence in Myanmar
- Hindi versions of the long-forms
- Hindus in Guyana and the Caribbean today

## Competitors
The watchlist's biggest videos this month are still Ramayana-film Shorts on channels much larger than Itiha. Two of them matter for this week's work.
- **Hindu Lifestyle**: "Boycott the Ramayana? What?"
  Why it worked: 111,833 views at 21.4x the channel's usual. It talks to one viewer and takes the side the crowd is not on: “If you plan on boycotting the new Ramayan movie, you might be doing more harm than good. Let me explain.”
  Steal: For Churchill: speak to the viewer who admires him, then hand him the document. “If you think Churchill saved the world, read what his Cabinet was told in 1943.”
- **The Sham Sharma Show**: "Bali Death Dark Truth"
  Why it worked: 614,246 views at 4.2x his usual, posted in the film's first week beside his other Ramayana-film Shorts, so very likely about the Ramayana's Vali, not the island.
  Steal: Nothing to copy. It is the reason the Bali video's title must say Indonesia: in India this month, “Bali” also means Vali.

Gaps
- The Emissary's Short “Why Did Japan Make Indian Propaganda Posters?” ran far above that channel's usual a month ago; nothing on Itiha covers it.
- Hindu Lifestyle's long-form “The Man Who Saved Hinduism in Trinidad” found a large audience; Itiha has only the Short “Ban on Hindu Marriages at Trinidad”.

## Trending now, make this
- **today, skip, 1/5**: Guru Nanak's birthday festival  
  Signal: His Wikipedia readership is 24.77x its usual in Hindi and 9.18x in English, and his name is trending on X. The festival has passed. (Wikipedia, X)  
  Make: Skip. A saint's life story is the kind of Short that does poorly here, and the date is gone. Do not read this spike as demand for the Tegh Bahadur Short either.
- **this_week, short, 2/5**: Two big films open on 4 December  
  Signal: Eetha, a biopic with Shraddha Kapoor, and Maatrubhumi: May War Rest in Peace, a war film with Salman Khan, both with trailers out. What either one is about is not confirmed in today's data. A third, Baba, is listed as historical but is unverified. (Release radar)  
  Make: Tomorrow, check what each film is about. If one tells a real event with a culprit who wronged Indians, script one Short on what the film leaves out, for 5 to 13 December: one person or one mystery, the villain in sentence one, about two minutes long to bring subscribers, judged on day three. If neither does, skip both. Three of the channel's four breakouts came from one film's release window.
- **this_week, short, 3/5**: Sati ban, 4 December, and the Ayodhya stone, 6 December  
  Signal: Both Shorts are already written. “The Year Britain Banned Sati, Englishmen Were Selling Their Wives” is sourced and not recorded; the second Irfan Habib Short, on the Treta-ka-Thakur inscription, was written on 1 November. (Calendar, scripts on disk)  
  Make: The Tegh Bahadur slot opens tomorrow; the Sati Short should take it because it is written. Record by 2 December and publish the morning of 4 December, after settling the “never wrote a law” line the script itself flags. Then the inscription Short on the morning of 6 December.
- **this_week, short, 3/5**: 14 December 1971: the killing of Bengal's intellectuals  
  Signal: Eighteen days out, two days before Vijay Diwas. The planning step falls on 30 November. The channel's 1971 heli-bridge Short is one of its best subscriber-earners among Shorts. (Calendar)  
  Make: Research this week who drew up the list and who carried it out, with names and the date; script a Short for the morning of 14 December. The channel's own failed 1971 refugee video left this lesson: “When the claim that makes the video unique is a cover-up, it goes in the first sentence, not at 60 percent.”
- **watch, skip, 2/5**: The Tipu Sultan row in Latur  
  Signal: Still in the news: a Congress MLA's remarks, a BJP protest, an FIR over a defaced poster, and his descendant asking for the textbook chapter back. (News)  
  Make: Skip. It is a party fight now, and party-politics Shorts do worst here; the Sonia Gandhi Short has no subscribers. The Tipu decision lapsed on 24 November; do not reopen it for this.

## Topic ideas (voltage-checked)
- [3/5, long] **Why British Trinidad Called Hindu Children Illegitimate**  
  Empire mechanism: a colonial state that shipped Indians in as indentured labour, then refused to recognise their Hindu marriages in law; check the year of the ordinance that ended it before scripting; Identity and religion stakes: children of Hindu marriages counted as illegitimate, with what that meant for inheritance; Villain plus hypocrisy: the same government that needed their labour denied their families  
  source: Hindu Lifestyle's Trinidad long-form found a large audience, Itiha has only a Short on it, and a viewer from Guyana is writing in. A guess: the channel's indenture long-form underperformed, and its lesson was to put the scene before the summary.
- [2/5, short] **The Japanese Posters That Told Indians Britain Was Finished**  
  Empire mechanism: one empire's propaganda aimed at another empire's subjects; Hidden history: wartime posters few Indians have seen  
  source: The Emissary's Short on the same subject ran far above its usual and nothing on Itiha covers it. Read the posters themselves; do not mirror their title. A guess.

## Instagram (separate platform, separate audience)
Instagram has 25,552 followers, up only 23 in the last 7 days, 3.3 a day. November's feed posts cannot be judged yet, because their follows keep arriving for about three weeks. Carousels still do the growing: their median reach is 3.69x that of reels.

Do more
- Write carousels that correct the record  
  50 revision carousels in the band converted a median 53.5 followers against 20.5 for the other lanes (40 posts). Median reach 15.9k vs 10.9k, conversion 3.77 vs 1.95 per 1k. 490 followers a month at stake.
- Build every carousel at 7-10 cards  
  The median carousel in the 7-10 band converts 34.5 followers (90 posts); outside the band, 12 (16 posts). Pooled rate 2.89 vs 1.85 follows per 1k reach — the band is not just reaching more people, it converts better per person reached, so this is not a reach artefact. 429 followers a month at stake.

Do less
- Stop making posts that get shared without bringing followers  
  19 of 103 rated posts are shared above the median (24.6/1k) but convert below it (2.1/1k): median 8.5k reach for a median 8 followers. The 33 posts that do both average 283 followers each. Share rate and follow rate correlate at only 0.39 — shareable and followable are separate skills, and the first one flatters itself on the home screen. 1,034 followers a month at stake.
- Stop posting single images  
  87 single images all time: 84.4k reach between them and 120 followers, 1.4 per post. A carousel in the 7-10 band averages 159.6. Every image slot is a carousel slot not taken. 94 followers a month at stake.

## Housekeeping
- **now**: Upload the Malay Ravana Short today: title starting “Ravana”, Related video set to the Indonesia long-form, its link in the pinned comment, and the text named on screen as the Malay “Hikayat Seri Rama”.  
  It has been written since 19 November and exists to send viewers to the Indonesia long-form while that video still draws them. Each day it waits, that audience is smaller. Whether a Short sends viewers on is a guess.
- **this_week**: Answer the fact-check comment under the Indonesia video with sources (/replies drafts it), and pin a correction if any point is wrong.  
  The Bali video goes to the same viewers; a fix made before it protects it.
- **later**: Test a new title and the designer's thumbnail on “The Church That Ran Britain's PRISON Camps” in Studio's Test & Compare.  
  Over the 365-day window it brings 34.3 subscribers per 1,000 views, the best on the channel, on only 1,079 views. That the title is the reason is a guess.
- **later**: Check in Studio why “How Jati's evolve organically ?” has 22 views since 3 November, and set GA4_PROPERTY_ID in .env so the brief can read itiha.info.  
  A public Short gets a few views a day, so this points to a setting, not the topic. Without the Analytics id, the site shows only its brand-name searches.
